Question: As part of an activity in the unit "Heat and Temperature", a teacher proposes the following reading to her Second Year High School students: "In the 17th century, many mining operations had reached such depths that pumping the accumulated water at the bottom had become a serious problem and the pumps that extracted the water had to be powered by horses or people. At this time, scientists like Torricelli or von Guericke made important advances related to atmospheric pressure, the existence of a vacuum, and the so-called "motive power of fire". The first to attempt to build a machine to lift water based on these advances was Papin, although his design was never constructed. More success was had by Savery, who developed a machine where a vacuum was created as the steam condensed. In 1712, Newcomen built a more practical machine, which, by not requiring such high steam pressure, was much safer, and was used for seventy years without requiring substantial improvements. The next step was taken by Watt, who, knowing Black's discoveries about latent heat, had the idea of separating the condenser from the body of the apparatus, constructing the first machine with this design in 1776. Watt's machine, cheaper and more efficient, ended up being used, in addition, in heavy metallurgy and the textile industry. This machine was exported from England to countries aspiring to industrialization, such as France, Germany, and Russia. This technology was the starting point for a revolution that continues to this day and enabled the development of more recent technological applications." Which of the following tasks can students perform from the reading of the previous text?

Answer B: Critically analyze scientific models, seeking their advantages and limitations in describing natural phenomena
Answer C: Develop examples, representations or analogies that allow them to link the contents of Physics with the understanding of everyday world phenomena
Answer D: Indicate how a dynamic and evolutionary process of knowledge construction is accounted for, and whose development is linked to the socio-historical context
Subdomain: Knowledge of teaching and instructional strategies

Question: A high school teacher is planning a class with the objective of "Describing the kinematics of uniform circular motions." Question: A third-grade teacher evaluated, in the unit on Natural Resources Care, the objective "Recognize the Rule of the 3Rs in concrete actions". To do this, she posed an activity in which the students had to write an everyday action for each corresponding category: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle. One of the students submitted the following response:  1. Use washable masks. 2. Plant plants in butter containers. 3. Separate and sort the containers that will be thrown away at home.  What feedback from the teacher would allow the student to be improved and guided towards achieving the proposed objective?
Answer A: Very good examples! But are all the Rs there? I invite you to answer these questions: What measure allows you to spend fewer resources or acquire only the essential? What new measure would you propose to complete your response?
Answer B: Very good examples! But are all the Rs there? I invite you to write the definition of each of the 3Rs: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, following the examples, and then answer this question: Which of these measures do you think is most effective in everyday life?

Answer D: Very good examples! But you missed an R. To complete the answer, I invite you to answer these questions: Why are these actions positive for the care of natural resources? To what extent do they contribute to reducing garbage and pollution on the planet?
Subdomain: Knowledge of assessment

Question: What activity is suitable for 3rd grade students to model the phenomenon of a solar eclipse and explain it to their peers?

Question: A lower nursery educator plans to gather evidence for the following evaluation indicator of the core area of Corporality and Movement: Identifies some parts of their body by pointing to them when named.
